issues.explanation: Pain Recall implies the patient personally sustained bodily injury during the trauma, which is hard to reconcile with the trauma type being trauma to a loved one unless there was also direct physical injury to the patient. That is not otherwise supported by the profile.

Physical Vulnerability and permanent bodily damage imply the patient believes his own body was physically harmed. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one presentation, this is difficult to explain clinically without evidence that he was also directly injured.

Military Topics is a trigger that suggests a military/combat-linked trauma context, but no other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal item supports a military-related formulation. As a standalone item it feels disconnected from the rest of the profile.

Avoid Driving is plausible for motor-vehicle trauma, but here it lacks support from the trauma type and from the rest of the profile. With no transport-related trigger or memory content, it appears to target a symptom domain not otherwise represented.

For trauma to a loved one, visible injuries is a plausible trigger, but darkness and alcohol smell are not well anchored to the rest of the profile. Nothing in memory, threat, or appraisals suggests a dark-space or alcohol-related trauma context, so these triggers feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent loved-one trauma presentation.

Avoiding work/study is hard to reconcile with this patient's occupation as a paramedic unless the trauma is clearly tied to the workplace, but the rest of the profile frames the trauma as harm to a loved one rather than occupational trauma. Drug use is also insufficiently supported elsewhere in the profile: there are no other items indicating broad externalising coping or substance-related trigger context, making this strategy feel tacked on.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but this specific wording implies a direct causal role in the event. The rest of the profile does not provide supporting content suggesting he believes his own actions caused the loved one's trauma. The other appraisals are about damage and unreliability of self, so this item is the least integrated with the stated trauma type and surrounding node content.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only trigger that suggests a substance-related context. The other trigger and memory items center on victims/injuries, which fits a paramedic exposed to injured loved ones or victims. Without any corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal content linked to alcohol, this item stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the trauma representation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Drug Use: take drugs
issues.explanation: Drug use can occur in PTSD, but here it is the only maladaptive strategy that implies substance misuse. The rest of the profile emphasizes work avoidance, suppression, sensory reliving, and hypervigilant threat responses. With no parallel alcohol/substance-related trigger, appraisal, or memory content, this item looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, self-blame is plausible only if the patient had a clear perceived role in failing to protect or respond. In this profile, the other items describe reliving of victims/injuries, hypervigilance, and damaged-self beliefs, but nothing else indicates a responsibility-based trauma narrative. This makes the specific self-blame item the least coherent appraisal relative to the rest of the selected content.

vignette:
Yousef, a 40-year-old married Middle Eastern man, came to treatment after nearly a year of trying to carry on as if nothing had changed. He worked as a paramedic, a job he had once experienced as steady and familiar, but that changed after a call involving a close family member. One evening, he was on duty when he received the kind of information every first responder dreads: a relative had been badly injured and was being brought in. By the time he arrived, the scene was already full of the details that now stayed with him—visible wounds, blood on skin and clothing, the sharp antiseptic smell of the hospital corridors, and the urgency of people speaking over one another. He found himself moving between professional response and the shock of seeing a loved one in that condition, and what he remembers most is the sudden collapse of the distance that usually let him function. In his telling, the event still does not feel like a finished memory; when it comes back, it returns as if he is there again, with the same terror in his body, the same sights and sounds crowding in at once.

Since then, Yousef has had moments when a reminder catches him without warning and the whole scene floods back. The sight of visible injuries on other people, even minor ones, can pull him into the same internal state, as if his mind has grabbed hold of the original incident and yanked him back into it. At times, a hospital or antiseptic smell is enough to make his stomach tighten and his attention narrow, because it carries him straight back to the place where he saw the injury and heard the voices around it. He described that when the memory returns, it does not arrive as a neat recollection but as a full sensory reliving: the smell, the light, the sight of wounds, and the emotional shock all seeming present at once. There are also parts of that night he cannot reconstruct no matter how hard he tries. He knows the broad outline, but there are gaps he cannot bridge, which leaves him unsettled and frustrated when he attempts to make sense of it afterward.

Yousef has come to believe that the event changed him in a lasting way. He said plainly that he feels permanently damaged, as if something in him did not return to baseline after that night. He also speaks with heavy self-blame, saying he should have protected others and failed, even though he can describe the situation as chaotic and beyond any one person’s control. He does not say this in a dramatic way; rather, it comes out as a quiet certainty that he fell short when it mattered. Alongside that, he has lost confidence in his own judgment and steadiness. He said he can’t rely on himself the way he used to, and that uncertainty now sits beneath many ordinary decisions.

In the months that followed, Yousef began to avoid work in a way that troubled him because it ran against everything he had always valued about himself. Some days he found it harder and harder to go in, knowing the hospital environment could bring him face-to-face with injuries or the smell that set him off. When he did force himself to show up, he often threw himself into tasks, staying busy so there would be no room to think. He described this as a deliberate effort to keep his mind occupied, to stop the memory from getting space. Even then, he found concentration difficult. During routine tasks, his attention drifted or snapped away, and he had to read things more than once or ask others to repeat themselves. At home, he kept trying hard not to think about the trauma, but the effort itself seemed to make the memory more present, as if holding it down took constant energy.

His sense of safety also changed in smaller, everyday ways. He always chooses where to sit based on how safe or protected he feels, scanning for the seat with a wall behind him or the clearest view of a room. He noticed this habit first in restaurants and waiting rooms, then at family gatherings, and later even in his own home when company was over. He also reacts with alarm when someone touches him unexpectedly, especially if he is already tense or absorbed in thought. His wife, who has tried to be patient, has occasionally startled him by touching his shoulder, and he recoils before he can stop himself, then feels embarrassed by the reaction.

By the time he sought help, the strain had become hard to hide. He was working less comfortably, avoiding parts of his job he had once handled without hesitation, and his attempts to stay occupied were no longer giving him the same relief. What finally brought him in was the sense that he could not keep living with the constant effort of pushing the memory away and arranging his world around reminders of that night. He hopes treatment will help him feel like himself again, or at least help him understand why he no longer trusts his own reactions. What he fears most is that the damage is permanent and that he will keep failing himself and others whenever something similar happens again.
